opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it's one where people's intuitions have shifted a lot over the last few years. There's this enormous amount of video of people doing things — cooking, folding laundry, assembling furniture — and it's very tempting to say, well, that's the internet-scale data for robotics, let's just learn from that.

I do think it's valuable, but I'd put it in a particular place. Observational data is really good for teaching a model about the world at a semantic level: what objects are, what tasks look like, what the sequence of steps might be, what a successful outcome looks like. That kind of high-level understanding transfers pretty well, and a lot of it already comes in through vision-language pretraining.

Where it's much weaker is the low-level physical part, the actual motor control. A human hand is very different from a parallel-jaw gripper, the dynamics are different, and critically, you don't observe the forces. You can watch someone fold a shirt a thousand times and still not know how hard they're pinching, or how they're reacting to the fabric slipping. That's the hard part of robotics, and it's largely invisible in video.

So my view is that robot data, data collected on the actual embodiment and ideally a lot of it across many embodiments, is still the thing that really moves the needle on dexterity and reliability. Human video is a complement. It can help with generalization, with understanding new tasks and new environments, maybe with providing some priors on motion. But I'd be skeptical of any plan that says we can skip collecting robot data and just learn from YouTube. In our own experiments, the robot data has been by far the most important ingredient, and the open question is how to get the most leverage out of the human data on top of that, not instead of it.

r001.rationale: The response says human hands differ from robot grippers and that video omits forces, but it does not clearly state that humans already possess low-level motor-control expertise that robots lack.

r002.rationale: It says data collected on the robot’s actual embodiment is what moves the needle on dexterity and reliability, clearly conveying the need for experience on the robot’s own body.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think it's really valuable, but it's also not a substitute for robot data. The way I think about it is that observational data of people, so videos of humans doing things, is incredibly abundant. There are millions of hours of it on the internet, and it captures a huge diversity of tasks, environments, objects, and ways of interacting with the world. If you only train on data collected directly on robots, you're very limited in how much coverage you can get, because collecting that data is slow and expensive, and you have to physically be there with the robot.

So human video gives you a lot of information about what tasks look like, how objects behave when you manipulate them, the sequence of steps involved in something like making a cup of coffee or folding laundry. It's a really rich source of priors about the physical world and about how tasks decompose.

The challenge is that there's a pretty big gap between watching a person do something and knowing how to actually do it yourself as a robot. The human has a different body, different hands, different kinematics. And critically, the video doesn't tell you the actions. You see the outcome of the person's motions, but you don't see the motor commands, the forces, the low-level control that produced them. So you're missing the thing that the robot ultimately needs to output.

The way I think this plays out is that human data is great for learning representations and higher-level understanding, like recognizing what state the world is in, predicting what happens next, understanding the structure of a task. And then you still need some amount of robot data to ground that in actual actions. The hope is that the human data lets you get away with a lot less robot data than you'd otherwise need, and it helps the robot generalize to situations it hasn't directly experienced.

There's also a more direct version, where you try to retarget human motion onto a robot, or you use egocentric video with hand tracking and treat the hand pose as a kind of pseudo-action. That can work reasonably well when the embodiment gap is small, like with dexterous hands, but it gets harder for robots that look very different from people.

So overall I'm quite optimistic about it. I just don't think it's the whole answer. The analogy I'd draw is that it's a bit like pretraining in language, where the internet gives you a tremendous amount of general knowledge, but you still need something more targeted to turn that into a system that actually acts well.

r001.rationale: The response says human video omits motor commands and forces that humans use, while robots need to produce those controls, identifying the low-level control gap.

r002.rationale: It says robot data is needed to ground learning in actions, but does not state that robots need experience through their own bodies to learn motor control.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of potential there, because people do a huge variety of things that we’d like robots to be able to do. And it’s much easier to collect video of a person doing something than to collect a robot successfully doing that same thing, especially when the robot doesn’t yet have the capability.

The challenge is that observing someone do a task doesn’t tell you exactly how to execute it. If you watch someone open a drawer, you can learn where they reach, how the drawer moves, and what success looks like. But you don’t necessarily observe the forces they apply or how they adjust their grip. And their hand and arm are different from the robot’s.

So I see human video as a really valuable source of information about tasks and the world, paired with robot interaction data that grounds that information in actions the robot can actually take. The interesting question is how much that observational data can reduce the amount of robot experience we need. I don’t think we should expect it to replace interaction entirely, but it could make learning from interaction much more efficient.

r001.rationale: The candidate notes that human hands and arms differ from robots and that video does not reveal forces or grip adjustments, but it does not clearly identify humans’ existing low-level motor-control expertise as a gap robots lack.

r002.rationale: It says human video should be paired with robot interaction data and that interaction can make learning more efficient, but it does not state that robots need experience from their own bodies to learn motor control.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a huge opportunity there, because people do a lot of things that we’d like robots to be able to do, and we can collect video of people much more easily than we can collect robots interacting with the world. You can learn a lot about what objects are, how they move, and what a successful task looks like just from watching people.

The challenge is that observation doesn’t directly tell you what action a robot should take. A person has a different body, and a video generally doesn’t tell you the forces they’re applying or exactly what’s happening at the contact between their hand and an object. Those details can matter a lot for manipulation.

So I think the interesting question is how to combine that broad observational data with robot experience. Can you learn useful representations and an understanding of tasks from human video, and then use a much smaller amount of robot data to ground that knowledge in the robot’s own actions? That seems like a really promising direction.

r001.rationale: The response notes that people and robots have different bodies and that video omits forces and contact details, but it does not say humans already have low-level motor-control expertise that robots lack.

r002.rationale: It recommends using robot experience to ground knowledge in the robot’s own actions, but does not state that robots need experience from their own bodies to learn motor control.
